claim: SOURCE NOTE: FETCH FAILED. Both mcp__fetch__fetch and WebFetch (retry) returned only page chrome and the author bio (Clark Boyd, 2024-06-18); article body not rendered. No claims extracted.
reason: Body not retrievable after one retry. Nothing may be cited from this URL.

claim: SOURCE NOTE: Shopify-app vendor blog; a paraphrase/rewrite of Mike King's Search Engine Land article (same section order, same 'fewer authors', 'dates in sync', 'SimilarWeb/Semrush' points). Names no attributes at all. No original analysis.
reason: Derivative of King, adds nothing, introduces errors (see H-entries). Cite King's original instead.

claim: SOURCE NOTE: Mirror/summary of Michael King's Search Engine Land article 'How SEO moves forward with the Google Content Warehouse API leak' (published 2024-05-30), compiled by trapilot.ai (an SEO tool vendor). Page says 'summary collected for reference'. Treat as King's claims, not trapilot's, and prefer the primary.
call: KEEP-WITH-CAVEAT (as a proxy for King only)
reason: Secondary summary of an original author; attribute names are fewer than in King's original.

modules: NavBoost, titlematchScore, bylineDate, syntacticDate, semanticDate, siteRadius, siteFocusScore, RegistrationInfo, avgTermWeight, badbacklinksPenalized, BlogPerDocData, docQualityScore
claim: SOURCE NOTE: Small web-dev shop blog (2024-06-02). Nearly entirely a condensed copy of Mike King's iPullRank/Search Engine Land takeaways, with first-person lines lifted from King ('In my own experience we have experimented...'). The attribute-list sections (Freshness onward) are King's iPullRank findings re-listed. Not original analysis.
call: KEEP-WITH-CAVEAT (attribute names only, verify against docs)
reason: Recycled from King. Its only added value is that it names attributes; the claims attached to them need checking against the hexdocs text.

claim: SOURCE NOTE: This URL is Part 1 (2024-05-29) of a series, an orientation post, NOT a module-by-module walkthrough. The module-by-module work is in the sibling posts ('What are attributes? Digging into the Google API docs', 'Navboost') which were linked but not fetched. Only four attribute names are mentioned, and none are explained.
call: KEEP (framing); no module-level detail available here
reason: Most epistemically careful of the five. Fetch the 'attributes' and 'Navboost' posts for module detail.

claim: The documents are not Google Search ranking algorithms and are not code used in Google's systems; they are API documentation for developers using Google Cloud's Content Warehouse.
reason: Conservative reading consistent with the docs being a generated client-library reference; best single framing in the set. Haynes derived it by googling 'contentwarehouse' and finding the Cloud product docs. Note: she only partly resolves why Search-flavoured attributes appear there.

claim: The package contains two lists: Attributes, and Modules (thousands, giving instructions for connecting to specific APIs on Google Cloud).
reason: Structural description of the hexdocs api-reference page; checkable. Also notes a shorter v5.0 exists, which matters for versioning.

claim: Haynes believes the attributes are all things that can be used in Google's calculations, and that ML systems adjust the weight given to each signal.
reason: She labels it 'my belief' and frames the series question as open ('are these used in ranking?'). The weighting claim is a general statement about ML ranking, not from the docs. Do not store as a finding.

claim: Some attributes relate to NavBoost, including navquery which uses NavBoost query data.
reason: Plausibly restates attribute doc text but no quote given; verify the exact module and field text before use.

claim: Clicks, including badClicks, are mentioned in the docs.
reason: Existence of field only; she makes no ranking-use claim. Verify containing module.

claim: PagerankWeight is documented as 'the weight to be stored in linkmaps for pageranker.'
reason: Direct quote of attribute description; checkable against docs.

claim: An AnchorSpamPenalizer attribute exists.
reason: Existence only, flagged with '!?!' surprise and no weight claim.

claim: Quality raters are mentioned in the docs ('interesting stuff about the quality raters'); the details were an embedded image not captured in the fetch.
reason: Content lost to an image in the fetch; no usable claim.

claim: Google announced at Cloud Next April 2024 that Gemini-based tools can be grounded in Google Search, which is why the Cloud docs may relate to Search systems.
reason: Reasonable context from a public announcement but the link to the leaked attributes is her hypothesis; no evidence in docs.

claim: The leak comprises 2,569 internal documents, 14,000+ features, roughly 8,000 related to Search.
reason: Counts are King's tallies; verify by counting attributes in hexdocs. Also note 'internal documents' conflicts with Haynes' finding that this is a public-style API reference; King's 'internal' framing is stronger than evidence.

claim: Google can specify maximum results per content format (e.g. limiting blog posts to three), a diversity limit.
reason: King's reading of a diversity-related attribute; the specific example of 'three blog posts' is illustrative, not documented as a value. Mirrors Endurtech and Hulk.

claim: Google measures the effort invested in content creation, potentially using LLMs to evaluate AI-generated material.
reason: Effort-score field existing is checkable; the LLM-evaluation clause is inference. Same for the separate UGC effort score.

claim: Page update significance affects crawl frequency and indexing decisions; changing dates alone no longer signals freshness.
reason: A significance attribute exists; 'no longer signals freshness' is an inference about history and behavior the docs cannot show.

claim: Documentation confirms Google penalizes bad backlinks (toxic backlinks).
reason: A field name does not confirm a penalty is applied in production, and the claim contradicts Google's public statements without evidence of use. 'Confirmed' is exactly the overreach to discard.

claim: Googlebot can execute POST, PUT and PATCH requests beyond GET.
reason: Likely restates a request-method enum in the docs; verify. Capability in the schema is not proof of crawl behavior.

claim: NavBoost click-based signals mean SEO and UX must align; users finding what they need and staying engaged matters.
reason: NavBoost's existence is backed by DOJ trial testimony, not by this leak alone; the UX conclusion is advice.

claim: Search Analytics should be viewed as diagnostic features: impressions far above clicks for a position predicts losing the ranking; performance thresholds exist per position.
reason: Asserts thresholds and a causal ranking mechanism with no quoted attribute. Presented as 'what we have learned' but is King's interpretation.

claim: Vector embedding analysis shows Google penalizes topic drift.
reason: Embedding-based site focus attributes exist; 'penalizes' is inference. Say 'measures', not 'penalizes'.

claim: Different ranking systems activate for different verticals, so experimentation is mandatory.
reason: Vertical-specific features (e.g. travel) are in the docs; 'no single best practice' is advice.

claim: Chrome data is integrated into search; clickstream tools (SimilarWeb) indicate where users go after leaving.
reason: Chrome-derived fields appear in the docs; whether used for ranking is not shown.

claim: Quality raters do feature engineering that trains classifiers, so 'gold standard' content subtly influences future updates.
reason: Causal chain to core updates has no basis in the docs.

claim: A 'smallPersonalSite' feature suggests Google is aware of small-site disadvantage and could boost them.
reason: Field exists; 'could boost' is speculation. Same pattern in Hulk's 'small sites disadvantaged' claim.

claim: Tactical: extend page titles beyond 60-70 characters because longer titles provide more ranking signals; the 60-70 limit is a myth.
reason: 'More ranking signals' is unsupported. Character limits govern display truncation; the leak doesn't change that. Conflicts with this agency's title-minimal-edit rules.

claim: Tactical: fewer authors with demonstrated expertise outperform freelance volume; synchronize dates across page, schema and sitemap; link relevance and traffic over volume; originality over length; careful with aged domains.
reason: Reasonable hygiene advice; none is proven by a leaked attribute. Date consistency and link relevance are low-risk.

claim: NavBoost is also called 'Glue', was uncovered in the DOJ antitrust trial, focuses on navigational queries, remembers clicks up to 13 months, and segregates by localization and device.
reason: Mostly DOJ trial testimony (Nayak/Grushetsky), not the leak. 'focused on navigation queries' is a narrow reading of the trial. Cite trial, not leak.

claim: With NavBoost, Google values clicks as one of the most important features; a click with no follow-up search, or a 5-minute dwell before returning, counts as success.
reason: 'One of the most important' is a weight assertion and the session-success definitions are King's inference, not documented.

claim: titlematchScore is believed to measure how well a page title matches a query.
reason: Name-based inference, explicitly hedged ('believed').

claim: Google looks at the byline date, the date in the URL, and on-page content dates.
reason: Matches attribute descriptions; the three-date model is the best-supported freshness claim in the set. Checkable. Does not prove freshness is a ranking factor.

claim: Google vectorizes pages and sites and compares page embeddings (siteRadius) to site embeddings (siteFocusScore) to judge whether a page is a core topic.
reason: Attributes exist and are documented as site focus and radius; the exact comparison description is King's. Also states 'learned definitively' in another bullet, which is overstated.

claim: Google stores domain registration information.
reason: Existence of the field only.

claim: Google measures the average weighted font size of terms in documents (and anchor text).
reason: Matches the attribute description; field exists, use unknown.

claim: There is a badbacklinksPenalized feature associated with documents, so toxic backlinks are real.
reason: Field name exists; 'indeed a thing' and 'penalized' as production fact is unsupported and conflicts with Google's public statements.

claim: BlogPerDocData has an undefined copycat score tied to docQualityScore, assumed to measure blog duplication.
reason: Author honestly flags 'without a definition' and 'my assumption'. Keep as a field-exists note only.

claim: Google scores documents for how commercial they are, which can stop a page being considered for informational queries.
reason: Commercial-score field plausible; the gating consequence is inference.

claim: Google uses vector embeddings to determine how far a page is from the rest of what a site discusses; this is 'learned definitively'.
reason: Fields exist; 'definitively' and upper-funnel conclusion overstated.

claim: Link value is higher from pages prioritized higher in the index ('flash memory'); pages with more clicks are likely in the flash tier; Google highly values link relevance.
reason: Index-tier attributes are real; link-value consequence is inference. Link relevance priority is reasoned advice.

claim: Google confirmed using Chrome data as part of the search experience.
reason: Contradicts earlier Google public denial; fields appear in docs but not their ranking use.

claim: Originality is measured in multiple ways and can yield a performance boost.
reason: Originality-score attributes exist; 'boost' is unsupported.

claim: There is no text-to-code ratio in the leaked docs even though SEO tools flag it.
reason: Absence claim from a search of the docs, plausible and useful, but absence in one API reference is not proof Google doesn't use it.

claim: Brand matters: build a notable, well-recognized brand outside Google search to broadly improve organic rankings.
reason: King's opinion; not a doc-derived claim.

claim: Quality raters do feature engineering for engineers to train classifiers, so write for a high rater score.
reason: Mechanism not shown in docs.

claim: Documents were unearthed by search marketer Erfan Amizi; 2,569 documents.
reason: Attribution of the leak origin (Erfan Azimi) is spelled 'Amizi' here, a transcription error; the number is from King.

claim: The leak reveals previously unknown features and ranking systems; the documents 'unveil an unprecedented glimpse into Google's ranking mechanisms' and define how Google uses page titles.
reason: Treats API reference as ranking-system disclosure, which Haynes' reading contradicts; 'defines how Google uses titles' not backed by any attribute.

claim: Google can cap the number of specific content types per SERP, so pivot to video if blog posts are capped.
reason: Recycled from King; see K2.

claim: The leak shows heightened importance of link relevance over volume of backlinks.
reason: 'Heightened importance' is a weight claim; leak has no weights.

claim: Google scores and boosts official travel sites; UGC quality is separately assessed.
reason: King's vertical-specific observations (travel, UGC); 'boosts' unsupported.

claim: Session success, post-site clickstream and click metrics are used; high ranking with low CTR signals a problem; recipe sites bury the recipe.
reason: Advice. The CTR diagnostic claim is King's, discarded in K8.

claim: Google can measure the quality of updates to a page; update significance tracked across dates in schema, sitemaps and on-page.
reason: Recycled from King; see K4.

claim: Documents suggest small sites are disadvantaged by inherent biases toward larger entities with more links and visibility.
reason: Not from the docs; recasting of King's 'smallPersonalSite' point into a bias claim.

claim: Optimize titles beyond 60-70 characters; append more targeted keywords.
reason: Same unsupported claim as K14.
